progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b13: primary, secondary and tertiary prevention; process, impact and outcome measures ("what we did, what people did, what the disease did"); judging secondary sources; no control group for SunSmart. From b14: genetic technology finds, chooses or changes; somatic gene therapy treats one person and does not change inheritance; a viral vector carries a working gene. From b16: the retina's light-sensitive cells. From b15: a cochlear implant bypasses damaged hair cells; access to sound, not normal hearing. From b11 (Module 8): a comparison group, chance and sample size. Not assumed: bowel screening kit details, colonoscopy and polyp (glossed in 2b), RPE65 (named on the card with its effect), percentage point (glossed in 2b by use).
progression.startsWith: This is the last Module 8 video, and it's practice. Evaluate questions in this module ask you to judge a prevention method or a technology, using evidence. Here are three HSC-style questions: a screening campaign, a gene therapy and a hearing technology. Pause and try each one properly, then we'll work through it together.
progression.stopsAfter: evaluating a bowel screening campaign (kit return is an impact measure; Region A rose 9 percentage points, the comparison region 2, so about 7 can be linked to the campaign; limits: no deaths data yet over two years, regions not randomised, over half still not screening; judgement: effective at raising screening, outcome not yet shown; improvement: long follow-up and targeting the lowest-return groups); explaining and evaluating RPE65 gene therapy (a viral vector delivers working genes to retinal cells, which make the missing protein; it aims to prevent further vision loss in one person, not inheritance; 13 of 20 against 0 of 10 with a control group; limits: small, short, one gene, needs living cells, costly; judgement: improved functional vision over one year for this gene fault, with degeneration not shown to stop; not population prevention); rejecting "implants fitted" as a process measure, choosing speech scores as the outcome measure, and evaluating cochlear implants (15 to 70 per cent in quiet, 5 to 35 in noise, 28 of 30 daily users; limits: noise, averages hide spread, one clinic, no comparison group; access: a nine-month wait, surgery and rehabilitation; judgement: highly effective in quiet, partly in noise); and the four-move decision board.
progression.nextLesson: none (last video in the Year 12 Biology playlist; scene 5 closes the course).

teaching.task: When an exam asks you to evaluate a prevention method or a technology from data, how do you get from the evidence to a judgement you can defend?
teaching.causalExplanation: Why kit return can prevent deaths (polyps removed, cancers found early; 2b); why the comparison region matters (other changes raise returns too; 2b, 2d); why the data can't show fewer deaths (they measure returns, not deaths; longer follow-up would test outcomes; 2c); how the vector restores vision (working gene, protein made, pigment remade; 3b); why gene therapy doesn't change inheritance (body cells only; 3b, 3d); why it needs living cells (3b); why the control group matters (it strengthens the evidence that the treatment caused the change, without proving chance impossible; 3c); why implants fitted is not effectiveness (process, not outcome; 4b); why speech scores match the disorder (4b); why averages mislead (spread; 4d).
teaching.conversationalApproach: This is the last Module 8 video, and it's practice. Question one. Start with how screening prevents harm. Now the limits. The classic mistake is saying the campaign raised returns by nine points. Question two. Explain first. Now the data. The classic mistake is writing that this gene therapy stops the disease being passed on. Question three. Thirty implants fitted is a process measure. Now the limits. The classic mistake is reading an average as if every patient improved that much. So for any evaluate question, use the same four moves.
teaching.openingDecision: This is the last Module 8 video, and it's practice. Evaluate questions in this module ask you to judge a prevention method or a technology, using evidence. Here are three HSC-style questions: a screening campaign, a gene therapy and a hearing technology. Pause and try each one properly, then we'll work through it together.

teaching.curriculumScope: - B8-IQ4-01: "use secondary sources to evaluate the effectiveness of current disease-prevention methods and develop strategies for the prevention of a non-infectious disease, including but not limited to:" with the examples "educational programs and campaigns" and "genetic engineering". Q1 evaluates a screening campaign from secondary data and proposes an improvement; Q2 evaluates a gene therapy (genetic engineering of body cells) from trial data.

design.visualSystem: One practice board throughout, in g01's layout: top-left the question card (stem, data and demands as an exam prints them, with the "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience" tag), readable through the whole question; the working fills the right two thirds; a type badge top-right ("Evaluate a campaign", "Evaluate a gene therapy", "Evaluate a technology"), hidden during each attempt. When the walkthrough starts, the card shrinks to a strip and each given is underlined in amber in the question text at the cue where it is used (no givens card). Earlier questions are cleared before the next card writes on. Throughout, a four-slot evaluation frame strip (b11's frame strip, b07's PathwayStrip in four-slot mode) sits under the working area and fills per question: "how it works", "what the evidence shows", "a real limit", "judgement". Q1's working is two coded paired bars (Region A and Region B, before and after) with a bracket for each change and a third bar for the difference, plus b13's three-level measure ladder (process, impact, outcome) as a grey recall. Q2's working is m8-eye-cutaway-v1.png with a callout zoom to the retina, the vector path (b14's m8-aav-vector-v1.png), b14's PreventedStrip ("symptoms, in one person" against "next generation"), and a dot grid of 20 and 10 (13 and 0 tinted). Q3's working is the measure ladder again (process against outcome), a coded before-after score chart (two pairs of bars, quiet and noise) and a small coded spread strip showing individual dots behind an average. No people, hands or faces: residents, trial participants and patients are words or plain coded dots only. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): besides the question strip, at most about three bright text items in the working area at once; each working tag fades when the next cue lands. Plates are scaled proportionally, never stretched.
